zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical reference: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510 (supplied page subset), CC BY 4.0. Consulted as a headword checkpoint after independent scan reading, not as a diplomatic transcription. Source: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ .

lines.note: Tateyoco is lengthwise and crosswise; the Portuguese pairs ao comprido with traues. The two orientations belong to one headword.
Tateyoxe is drawing a door partly shut. The listed suru form and the example below are historical forms, not a reason to replace the printed principal parts.
Touo tateyoſuru illustrates partly closing the door; ta completes Portuguese por-ta. The upright Japanese follows the italic example marker Vt.
Tatǒgami denotes folded paper, here gilded or decorated. Preserve the visible caron and the printed terminal hyphen after com, even though com is a complete preposition.

runs.text: pinturas em que as molheres metem poſturas, ou

lines.note: The decorated paper holds women's cosmetics or other belongings. Poſturas belongs to this material-use description, not a Japanese example.

runs.text: varias couſas. ¶ Item, Papel dobrado que

lines.note: The first description ends with assorted things; the paragraph mark introduces another use of folded paper. Its location is completed by the next row.
The paper is carried in the bosom of one's clothing. This short continuation completes the second explanation of Tatǒgami.
Tatoi is introduced as a concessive conjunction meaning even though. The statement that it precedes another expression continues below.
The dictionary says Tomo follows Tatoi. Tomo is consequently a Japanese grammatical term embedded in Portuguese, whereas Tatoi toqi u- begins a separate Japanese example.
The example continues utsuri, koto sarutomo: even though time and circumstances pass. Preserve its physical division after u- and the visible long s in ſarutomo.
Po completes Portuguese tem-po; the rest says that everything passes. The translation completes the concessive example rather than adding a new sense.
Tatoye means comparison; tatoye wo hiku illustrates bringing forward a comparison or analogy. The following row supplies its Portuguese translation.
Trazer algũa comparação translates adducing a comparison; a second expression, Tatoyeuo toru, begins after the paragraph mark.
Toru completes tatoye wo toru. Idem explicitly gives it the same comparison-making meaning as the preceding expression.
The verb means to compare. Eccle- begins Ecclesia inside a Japanese sentence; the scan shows upright letters throughout, not the OCR's alternating italic fragments.
Ecclesia wo ten no kuni ni tatoyuru compares the Church to the kingdom of heaven. The Japanese object particle follows the divided loanword Ecclesia.

runs.text: a Igreja ao reino do ceo.

lines.note: The Portuguese completes the comparison between the Church and the heavenly kingdom. Preserve ceo rather than replacing it with modern céu.
Tatoyeba and the alternative tatouaba introduce an example or comparison. The latter spelling is retained as printed rather than regularized to the preceding form.

runs.text: ção, ou trazendo exemplo, ou aßi como, &c.

lines.note: The gloss offers making a comparison, giving an example, or saying just as. It completes compara-ção across the physical line break.

Tatta is equated with tada and said to have several meanings. Both the headword and the examples support tt rather than OCR Taita. The small mark in ſignificaçòes is indistinct; the draft's grave-accent reading is retained as a nonblocking graphic caveat.
Tatta hitokai wo fukoozu expresses an intention to blow only once. The scan supports fitocaiuo and fucǒzu, correcting OCR ſitocaiuo and focǒzu; the prospective ending is historical.

The Portuguese completes the one-time sounding example; bazio is retained as the printed-looking spelling in the shell-horn context. Tattamononi xemuru starts an example of doing nothing but pressing or attacking.

runs.text: Não fazia ſe não apertar, ou combater.

lines.note: Ru completes xemuru. The Portuguese says that he did nothing but press or fight; combater restores the damaged vowel and the coherent word in place of c mbater.
Tattǒ is explained through michi ni tassuru, attaining mastery in a discipline. The gloss continues the fields in which such perfection is attained.
The fields include arts and study. Tattǒno nin describes a master of such a discipline; the scan supports nin rather than OCR min and repeats the headword's tt.
A person accomplished in an art completes the Japanese example. The damaged final letter in algũa is read as a, agreeing with the visible feminine arte, not OCR algũs.
Tattoi describes something holy, praiseworthy, or blessed. This religious and honorific range is kept distinct from the preceding mastery entry.
Tattô is the adverbial form associated with tattoi. Its upward circumflex is visible and is not assimilated to the caron in Tattǒ above.
Tattoſa is the corresponding abstract noun, the quality of being revered or venerable. The standalone form occupies its own indented physical row.
Tattomi means venerating or honouring. Its listed contracted past ending ôda is preserved as historical morphology rather than replaced by a modern form.
The example says that when one deeply honours the lord, one should also honour his retainer. The verb is tattomeba, not OCR tatromeba; vya- continues uyamau across the break.
The Japanese finishes with a reason for honouring the retainer; Tac. is the upright source label. Honrando mui- begins the Portuguese rendering, whose next row completes muito.

runs.text: to ao ſenhor, ha razão pera tambem eſtimar a

lines.note: The translation explains that honouring the lord gives reason also to esteem his servant. Preserve the separate preposition a at this row's end.
O criado completes the object of estimar a from the previous row. This short continuation is substantive body text, not furniture.
Tattomiai describes multiple people joining in worship or reverence. The two caroned contracted endings remain distinct from the preceding verb's circumflex.
Many people revering something completes the plural-action gloss. The line also finishes reuerẽ-ciar, preserving the printed nasal abbreviation.

runs.text: Parte da ladeira, ou coſta q̃

lines.note: Taua, alternatively tauo, denotes the less steep portion of a hillside or slope. The abbreviation q̃ introduces the relative clause continued below.
Tauo wo koyuru is crossing the gentler slope. The entire Portuguese Su- is italic and begins subir; the OCR wrongly assigned its hyphen to roman type.

runs.text: bir, ou paſſar algũa ladeira deſcanſada.

lines.note: The example is translated as ascending or crossing an easy slope. The printed two long s letters in paſſar and the physical word division are retained.
Tauabure means play or jest. Tẽ- begins the Japanese tenshi, with an abbreviation tilde; its letters are upright, not partly italic as in the draft.

Tenshi ni tawabure no kotoba nashi says that the sovereign has no frivolous words. The second-pass enlargement distinguishes a small word gap between Rey and não, restoring the separation in the Portuguese statement.

runs.text: diz palauras leues, ou de zombaria.

lines.note: The king does not utter light or jesting words. Diz and palauras correct the OCR's dez and pelauras; the historical u spelling is retained.
The verb tauabure means to joke or play amicably. Its first Portuguese adverb is physically divided after a-.
Migauelmente completes amigauelmente. The Japanese example says that a small butterfly plays among the flowers; ta- begins the repeated verb.
The Japanese verb completes tauabururu; the Portuguese describes the little butterfly playing. Brin- is fully italic and ends in a hyphen, not the OCR's detached roman n and full stop.

runs.text: cando, ou pouſando pollas fullas, ou flores.

lines.note: The butterfly plays or alights among leaves or flowers. Preserve the printed-looking fullas rather than silently modernizing it to folhas.
The final paragraph adds a figurative sexual sense, fornication. It belongs to the same verb and remains a separate physical body row.
Tauacoto means foolish talk or nonsense. The divided Ta- begins the example containing the same noun rather than a separate entry.
Tawagoto wo yuu is speaking things out of place or to no purpose. The Portuguese explains the pragmatic sense of the utterance.

runs.text: Tauame, uru, eta. i, Tauome, uru.

lines.note: Tauame is equated with tauome, a transitive bending verb. En- begins the Portuguese entortar and must remain on this physical row.

runs.text: tortar, ou dobrar como bambu, pao, &c.

lines.note: The gloss completes bending or making crooked, with bamboo and wood as examples. This is an action upon an object, not the later intransitive bending entry.
The noun Tauamure explicitly refers to Tauabure, the earlier play or jest entry. The difference between m and b is preserved, not harmonized.
The corresponding verb likewise points to Tauabure, uru. This separate cross-reference preserves the distinction between the noun and verbal entries.
Tauaqe means to act foolishly or become a fool. The example starts ta-waqeta mono, a person who has behaved foolishly.
Tawaketa mono and tawake are alternative descriptions of a fool. The scan supports Paruoeirão, not OCR Parnoeirão; the Portuguese continues with a synonym below.
Tolo completes the pair of Portuguese words for a fool. It is a short continuation of the preceding example, not another headword.
Tauaqemono is independently glossed as a fool or simpleton. Its mono element is part of the headword rather than a Portuguese explanation.
Tauara is a bale or sack for rice, wheat, and similar goods. Darroz is retained with the printed contraction and spelling.
Tauarago is equated with Namaco and described as an edible marine slug. The definition identifies the Japanese food name without requiring a modern species assignment.
The marine animals are eaten in Japan. This completes the definition of Tauarago/Namaco without extending it to unrelated sea slugs.
Tauareme is equated with keisei and glossed as a prostitute or courtesan. The closing P. is an upright poetic-usage label, not part of the italic Portuguese gloss.
Tauo sends the reader back to Taua above, the gentler part of a slope. The cross-reference does not supply an additional sense.

runs.text: Tauomacaxi, ſu, l, tauomaxi, ſu, aita.

lines.note: Tauomacaxi and tauomaxi are alternative causative bending forms. Do- starts dobrar and is wholly italic; the OCR's isolated roman o was spurious styling.

runs.text: brar, ou entortar como cana, ramo, &c.

lines.note: The physical meaning is bending or twisting a cane, branch, or similar object. The following example extends this action figuratively to a person's heart.
Hito no kokoro wo tawomasu, alternatively tawomakasu, means inclining someone's heart. The second alternative is divided after tauo-.

runs.text: Inclinar o coração dalguẽ a algũa

lines.note: Macaſu completes the alternative verb. The Portuguese says to incline someone's heart toward something, with the destination noun continued below.
Couſa completes the object of the inclination. This single-word continuation belongs to the preceding psychological example.
Tauome is assigned the same bending meaning by Idem. Its separate headword also supplies the target of the cross-reference near the top of the column.
Tauomi describes the wood or branch itself bending, contrasting with the preceding transitive forms. Preserve the circumflex in its contracted past ending ôda.
Tauore means falling to the ground. Its historical ruru principal form is retained; the paragraph mark introduces a figurative application below.

runs.text: permet. Cair de ſeu estado, renda, &c.

lines.note: The figurative sense is falling from one's standing, estate, or income. The compressed permet. is retained as printed rather than expanded in the transcription.
Shinshoo ga taoruru illustrates the ruin of someone's estate or standing. The Portuguese confirms this financial or social collapse, not a literal person falling.
Tauorecacari means being on the point of falling. The complement describing where the object may fall continues on the following row.

runs.text: cair no chão, ou ſobre outra, &c.

lines.note: The object may fall onto the ground or onto another object. This completes the impending-fall sense, distinct from the next entry's actual piling-up collapse.
Tauorecaſanari describes falling one upon another. The Portuguese begins the singular example and divides ſo-bre at the line end.

runs.text: bre outra, ou hũs ſobre os outros.

lines.note: The explanation expands from one thing falling on another to several falling upon each other. The worn conjunction is read as ou rather than OCR cu; the first vowel is weak.
Tauorefuxi means falling prostrate. The printed ita ending belongs to the listed historical forms and is not expanded to a modern past tense.
Tauori is breaking something off by hand. Its example objects, branches and flower sprays, follow on the next row.

runs.text: ramos de aruore, ou raminhos de flores com

lines.note: The objects are tree branches or small flowering twigs. Com continues into a mão below, specifying the means of breaking them.
The action is performed by hand; hana wo taoru illustrates plucking or breaking off flowers. The Japanese example and the Portuguese description are mutually consistent.
Tauoxi is toppling something such as a tree. Preserve the historical principal part oita rather than substituting a modern -shita ending.
The objects are things standing upright. Taiboku wo kiri-taosu begins an example of cutting down a large tree, divided after qiri-.
Tauoſu completes the compound verb. The Portuguese likewise describes felling a large tree by cutting it; cortan- continues onto the next row.

runs.text: doo. ¶ Item, permet. Dar com alguem

lines.note: Doo completes cortandoo, cutting it down. The new figurative paragraph turns from felling trees to bringing about someone's downfall.
The gloss explicitly explains the idiom as destroying someone. Neijinua fitouo begins a Japanese example concerning malicious flatterers and their victims.
Ii taosu describes ruining someone through speech. The Portuguese identifies the agents as flatterers and malicious people; deſ- continues destruir across the break.
Truem completes deſtruem: they destroy others. The separate a os is retained as printed and belongs to this figurative example.
Tauoyaca describes something refined, lovely, soft, and graceful. The final coordinated adjective continues below.
Gracioſa completes the description of graceful softness. This is not the beginning of the following adjectival headword.
Tauoyacana is given the same meaning as tauoyaca by Idem. The added na belongs to the Japanese adjectival form.
Tauoyacani is the adverb, glossed as acting gracefully or with refinement. Adu. is part of the italic grammatical apparatus.
Tauoyacaſa names the corresponding quality of grace or softness. The form is printed alone on an indented row.

Tavzzura is explicitly said to be eaten. The unusual-looking Rũa is retained; it appears intended as the Portuguese frog word, but the vowel is poorly formed. NINJAL's supplied entry 243b23 corroborates the headword, not this gloss; an external lexical search did not resolve it further.
Taxacu is borrowing another person's property, explained by tano mono wo karu. Tomar empreſ- is wholly italic and continues as emprestada on the next page; its catchword is separate furniture.
